report:
Conclusion: the claim is **supported**, not false. In the phase 3 ACTIVE randomized trial, daily subcutaneous abaloparatide 80 µg for 18 months significantly reduced new vertebral fractures versus placebo in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis; the published conclusion states it reduced both new vertebral and nonvertebral fractures over 18 months (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27533157/). Contemporary summaries report about an 86% relative reduction in new vertebral fractures, roughly a 3.6 percentage-point absolute reduction versus placebo.

Regulatory labeling reflects this: FDA’s Tymlos label indicates abaloparatide for postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at high fracture risk and carries the class warning about rat osteosarcoma, so use is targeted rather than universal (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2017/208743lbl.pdf).

A network meta-analysis also found abaloparatide reduces vertebral and nonvertebral fracture risk versus placebo and compares favorably with several options, though indirect comparisons have uncertainty (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6614166/). ACTIVExtend suggests benefit is maintained when abaloparatide is followed by alendronate, but it was not a direct head-to-head antiresorptive comparison (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7112966/).

Caveats: evidence is strongest for high-risk postmenopausal women over 18 months; it does not prove superiority for every patient, and cost, injection burden, hypercalcemia, and safety warnings matter.
